mcqs.question: A low-priority thread holds a lock that a high-priority thread needs. What is this scenario called, and why is it a real concern?
options: The ABA problem, since the lock's value looks unchanged
A goroutine leak, since the low-priority thread never releases anything
Priority inversion — the high-priority thread is effectively forced to wait on the lower-priority one, which grounded the Mars Pathfinder rover in a real historical incident
A deadlock, since both threads are permanently blocked
mcqs.explanation: Priority inversion is exactly this scenario — a high-priority thread's progress becomes gated by a lower-priority thread it shouldn't logically depend on, a real and historically documented failure mode. It isn't the ABA problem (unrelated to CAS), not a goroutine leak (a CSP-specific term), and not a deadlock unless both threads are mutually blocked on each other.

mcqs.question: What makes compare-and-swap (CAS) usable as a lock-free building block with no separate lock involved?
options: It is implemented as a single atomic hardware instruction, so the check-and-write happens as one indivisible step
It always succeeds on the first attempt, so retries are never needed
It automatically acquires a lock internally before executing
It only works on single-threaded programs
mcqs.explanation: CAS's atomicity is a hardware guarantee — the compare and the write happen as one indivisible operation — which is exactly why no separate lock is needed to make it safe under concurrent access. It doesn't always succeed on the first try (retries are the whole point of the pattern), doesn't secretly use a lock, and is specifically useful under multithreading.

mcqs.question: In the lock-free counter's CAS retry loop, what happens if `compareAndSet(old, next)` returns false?
options: The program throws an exception and terminates
The counter's value is permanently corrupted
The thread blocks until the lock is available
The loop re-reads the current value and retries the computation, since another thread changed the value first
mcqs.explanation: A false result means another thread's CAS succeeded first, so this thread simply re-reads the now-current value and tries again — no blocking, no corruption, no exception, since retrying is the entire mechanism by design. There is no lock involved for the thread to block on in this pattern.

mcqs.question: A lock-free stack's CAS on the top pointer succeeds because the pointer value looks unchanged from what was last read — but a node was actually popped and a new node was allocated at the same address in between. What problem is this?
options: The ABA problem — CAS only checks whether the value looks the same, not whether something happened in between
A deadlock caused by lock ordering
A goroutine leak from an unclosed channel
Priority inversion between two threads
mcqs.explanation: This is the textbook ABA problem: CAS's "still equal" check can pass even though the underlying data changed and changed back, which is dangerous specifically when memory addresses get reused. It has nothing to do with lock ordering, channels, or priority scheduling.

mcqs.question: What makes Software Transactional Memory more composable than lock-based code, according to this topic?
options: STM transactions run without any conflict-checking, so they never need to retry
STM disables garbage collection during a transaction

Combining two STM transactions typically just means wrapping them together, since the retry-on-conflict machinery handles composition automatically — unlike combining lock-protected operations, which risks new deadlocks
STM only works for read-only operations
mcqs.explanation: STM's optimistic retry mechanism absorbs the complexity of combining operations, avoiding the lock-ordering reasoning that combining separate mutex-protected sections requires. STM transactions do check for conflicts and can retry, don't disable GC, and support writes as well as reads.

mcqs.question: A team decides to hand-write a new lock-free data structure for a moderately complex use case instead of using a battle-tested library implementation. What is the most accurate characterization of this decision?
options: A routine engineering task any competent developer can complete correctly on the first attempt
Unnecessary risk — lock-free correctness involves subtleties like the ABA problem, memory reordering, and torn reads that are notoriously easy to get wrong and hard to catch in review or testing
Guaranteed to be slower than the equivalent lock-based version
Only a concern on older CPU architectures, irrelevant on modern hardware
mcqs.explanation: This topic frames hand-rolled lock-free code as a specialist skill precisely because these bugs are subtle, timing-dependent, and can survive testing and review while still being wrong under specific concurrent conditions. It's not routine, isn't guaranteed slower or faster, and memory reordering concerns are very much present on modern hardware.
